title: Bridging the Divide
author: Knowledge For Teachers
summary: Knowledge For Teachers uses a family science fair, where specialists from different fields cheerfully deferred to one another's expertise rather than guarding disciplinary turf, as a model for how educational research should but rarely does operate. The piece argues that cognitive science, neuroscience, and behavioural science each answer a genuinely different classroom question (what the mind can hold and retrieve, what biological conditions make learning possible, what learning looks like as observable action) and that treating any one of them as sufficient, or worse, using a brain scan to "prove" a teaching method works, produces exactly the kind of overreach that mutates into toxic neuromyths like learning styles and Brain Gym. Working through concrete classroom examples, including a worked side-by-side comparison of two students' responses to the same maths problem analyzed through all three lenses, the author shows how each discipline surfaces a different diagnostic question a teacher can ask about the same struggling student rather than competing to be the single correct explanation. The argument closes by reframing the practical payoff: teachers don't need one discipline to win, they need the habit of asking better questions before labelling a student as lazy, anxious, or incapable, because the answer will not always come from the same field.
points: The organizing metaphor, education research as an 'academic archipelago' of disciplines that study the same students but describe problems differently, reframes interdisciplinary disagreement as a structural feature to navigate rather than a dispute to resolve in favor of one field.

The piece names a specific methodological trap in neuroscience-in-education claims: 'pointing to a brain scan to prove a teaching method works is a bit of a trap,' since Bowers's point that 'all learning changes the brain' means any activity will show up on a scan, brain activity alone can't validate instructional choice.

The side-by-side worked example, the same open-ended maths problem analyzed through cognitive science (schema access), neuroscience (cortisol stress response), and behavioural science (insufficient antecedent instruction) for two different students, operationalizes the abstract three-lens argument into something a teacher could actually use diagnostically.

Julie Vargas's reframe, 'You never make an error... An error is a faulty contingency; it is not something in you,' is used to model the behavioural-science habit of locating the explanation for student struggle in instructional conditions rather than in a fixed trait of the student.
quotes: One moment that stuck with me was when a child asked a question and the scientist responded with, I know a little bit about that, but you should ask that person over there. There was no embarrassment in admitting that his knowledge had limits.

Cognitive scientists, neuroscientists and behaviour scientists are often looking at the same students and worrying about similar problems. Yet they may describe those problems differently, collect different kinds of evidence and work at different levels of explanation.

There is also a fundamental logic problem when we try to force brain science into the classroom. Because of this massive gap in complexity, pointing to a brain scan to prove a teaching method works is a bit of a trap.
When we ignore this gap, complex science gets rushed into schools by commercial vendors and mutates into toxic neuromyths like learning styles theory or Brain Gym.
You never make an error. You were doing what the laws of behavior are predicting you would do under those contingencies. An error is a faulty contingency; it is not something in you.
We do not need one discipline to win. Teachers need better explanations, better measures and better ways to decide what to do next.
